knowledge.name: Bronchiectasis
knowledge.description: A chronic lung condition in which damaged airways become abnormally widened and have impaired mucus clearance, predisposing to persistent sputum production, recurrent infections and repeated exacerbations.
risk_factors: Previous severe or recurrent respiratory infections
physical_examination: Signs of hypoxemia or respiratory compromise in advanced disease
recommended_investigations: Sputum culture including evaluation for clinically relevant bacterial or mycobacterial infection
Blood tests for infection and possible underlying causes
Further etiologic testing such as cystic fibrosis or immune evaluation when clinically indicated
red_flags: Sepsis or rapidly worsening systemic illness
contraindications: Do not rely on a normal or non-diagnostic chest X-ray alone to exclude bronchiectasis; CT is the key confirmatory imaging test.

knowledge.name: Acute Exacerbation of COPD
knowledge.description: An acute, sustained worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond the patient's usual stable COPD state. Common manifestations include increased breathlessness, cough, sputum volume and/or sputum purulence. Exacerbations may be triggered by infections, smoking-related exposure, air pollution or other causes and are not always bacterial.
common_symptoms: Change in sputum colour or purulence
associated_symptoms: Fever or systemic symptoms when infection is present
risk_factors: Previous COPD exacerbations or hospital admissions
Air pollution or respiratory irritant exposure
recommended_investigations: Chest X-ray when severe disease or an alternative diagnosis is suspected
Arterial blood gas testing in severe exacerbation or suspected respiratory failure
Sputum culture when clinically indicated, particularly with purulent sputum or poor response
ECG when cardiac disease or another cardiopulmonary cause is suspected
red_flags: Signs of respiratory failure or sepsis
contraindications: Do not assume every COPD exacerbation is bacterial; antibiotic decisions require clinical assessment.
Avoid uncontrolled oxygen administration in patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure; oxygen should be clinically titrated.
